title: Why lineage matters
hookLine: teaching passed person to person, checked and handed on

cards: Who taught the person who taught you to ride a bike? The answer may be a blank.
But in a Zen hall, at certain ceremonies, people chant a long list of names: teacher, and teacher's teacher, back and back, until the list reaches the Buddha.

In a Tibetan monastery, before a text is studied, a teacher may read it aloud so the students receive it the way the teacher once received it. A family tree, but of teaching. Why would anyone bother keeping it?

teach.h: THE DHAMMA WILL BE YOUR TEACHER.
teach.b: Lineage means the chain of people a teaching has passed through.
In the Pali Canon, as the Buddha is dying, he tells Ananda not to think the disciples will be left without a teacher: the Dhamma and the discipline he taught will be their teacher after he is gone.
So the teaching itself is the center.
But it has to be carried, and people carry it. Monastic ordination, as the day on the nuns showed, is handed on by those who already hold it.
A Zen teacher receives permission to teach from their own teacher, who checks their understanding first.
Tibetan teachers speak of receiving a transmission, a reading or an empowerment, from someone who received it before them. Why keep track?
Partly quality control: a teaching tested by a teacher who was tested by a teacher has been checked again and again. Partly honesty: you can say where your teaching came from.
And partly gratitude: the names in the chant are people who kept the lamp lit. But here's the balance, and it comes from the Buddha too.

teach.h: PARAMPARA: NOT PROOF ON ITS OWN.
teach.b: In his talk to the Kalamas, one thing he tells them not to rely on alone is parampara, the chain of tradition handed down. A lineage on its own doesn't prove a teacher is good, as yesterday made clear.
It gives you a way to check; the conduct is still the test. Schools weigh lineage differently; some put it at the center, some keep it quietly in the background. Either way, the names are kept.

how: Zen communities chant the names of their lineage ancestors, Tibetan teachers give reading transmissions and empowerments received from their own teachers, and monastic ordinations are conferred by monks or nuns who already hold them.

games.q: the Buddha is dying. some may think, he tells Ananda, that they will have no teacher now. who does he say their teacher will be?
o: the Dhamma and the discipline will be their teacher
they should find a new master
games.why: the Buddha points away from any one person, to the teaching and the discipline he left.

practice: Think of someone who taught you something that matters, a skill, a way of being, a kind of patience, and then step back one link to whoever taught them, even if you don't know their name.
Step back once more, if you can, and picture that person however dimly. Let a little thanks run back along the chain, link by link, to people you'll never meet.

wordCard.voice: Parampara. The chain of teachers handed down person to person, checked along the way, and honored, though never proof on its own.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit parampara: a succession, a chain handed down.

carryVoice: Your line: handed on. The teaching is the teacher; people carry it. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), the Dhamma and Vinaya as teacher
